passage:
"Chinmay, it's eleven. You haven't eaten."
"I'm not hungry, Thomas. The placement test is in nine days."
"You said that yesterday. Dal's still warm. Five minutes."
"...Fine."
Chinmay ate standing up. Thomas, his cousin, leaned on the fridge.
"Tomorrow, walk with me to the vegetable market at seven."
"I need to study."
"Twenty minutes. You'll study better. You've been rereading one page for an hour."
Next morning, grumbling, Chinmay went. The day after, he went without being asked.
On the sixth night, he shut the laptop at 11:30. "I still don't feel like doing anything, you know. But I'm sleeping."
"That's the point."
"If it doesn't get better after the test, I'll see the college counsellor."
"I'll come with you if you want."

qa.q: Where did Thomas ask Chinmay to walk at seven?
qa.a: To the vegetable market.

qa.q: What does "I still don't feel like doing anything" tell us about Chinmay?
qa.a: He is still stressed and low on motivation. He keeps the routine anyway, which shows he is choosing it rather than waiting to feel ready.

qa.q: On which day did Chinmay start going on the walk without being asked, and why does that choice matter?
qa.a: The day after his first grumbling walk. Choosing it for himself shows the routine was becoming his own, not something Thomas pushed on him.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel when Chinmay mentions the college counsellor?
qa.a: Thomas would likely be relieved that Chinmay knows when to get more help. Offering to go along shows Thomas wants to support Chinmay without carrying it all alone.

grounding: A young man under exam stress keeps meals, sleep and a daily walk going with his cousin's help, and plans to see a counsellor if it does not improve.

passage: My name's Yogesh, and the month my father was in hospital I learned something small. I was a nineteen-year-old boy in second-year B.Com, travelling between the ward and college, and everything felt grey. I didn't want to cook, sleep or do anything. My friend Dhruv didn't give me advice. He just texted every night at ten: "Lights off in thirty?" So I made three rules I could keep even on bad days. Eat something real at lunch, even canteen poha. Walk from the station instead of taking the auto. Lights off by 11. Some nights I lay awake anyway. But the days stopped blurring. I could sit with Papa and actually listen. Once, when I felt heavy for weeks, I did go to the college counsellor, and I'm glad I did. The rules didn't fix everything. They gave me a floor to stand on.

qa.q: What were Yogesh's three rules?
qa.a: Eat something real at lunch, walk from the station instead of taking the auto, and lights off by 11.

qa.q: What does Yogesh mean when he says the rules gave him "a floor to stand on"?
qa.a: He felt that even when everything was grey, the basic routine kept him steady. It did not remove the sadness, but it stopped him from sinking further.

qa.q: When the heaviness lasted for weeks, what choice did Yogesh make, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He went to the college counsellor. Routines help, but lasting distress needs someone qualified, and he did not try to push through alone.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt sending the same text every night?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt a bit helpless about Yogesh's father, so a simple nightly text was a way to care without prying. Seeing Yogesh steadier would have been reassuring.

grounding: A young man with a sick father keeps simple rules about meals, walking and sleep, and sees a counsellor when heaviness lasts.

passage:
Warden's note, Block C, 14 March
I've noticed Chaitanya (Room 212) looking drained since the internship rejection last week. He was skipping mess dinner, and his light was on at 3 a.m. two nights running. I didn't lecture. On Tuesday I asked if he'd join the 6:30 walk round the ground that a few of us do. He came, silent, hands in pockets. Wednesday he came again. By Friday he'd started eating at the mess and said, "I'm still low, sir, but I'm sleeping by midnight." I told him that keeping his basics going on flat days was a real skill, and that if the low mood stays or gets heavier, the campus counsellor and doctor are there, and I'll walk over with him. He nodded. I'll keep checking in quietly.
Lalit, Warden

qa.q: What time was Chaitanya's light on two nights running?
qa.a: His light was on at 3 a.m. two nights running.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's "I'm still low, sir, but I'm sleeping by midnight" show about how he feels?
qa.a: He is still disappointed about the rejection, but he is proud or at least relieved that he is keeping his sleep steady despite the low mood.

qa.q: Lalit could have lectured Chaitanya. What did he choose instead, and why did it work?
qa.a: He invited him on the 6:30 walk and let him come silently. A gentle, repeated routine helped more than advice would have.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Lalit's offer to walk over to the counsellor with him?
qa.a: It likely makes getting help feel less scary and less shameful, because someone he trusts would go with him.

grounding: A hostel warden notes how a stressed student keeps walks, meals and sleep going, and points him to the counsellor if distress lasts.

passage:
Saturday, 10:30 p.m.
Day nine of this. Final-year project crashed, Appa and Amma arguing on every phone call, and all I want is to lie on the bed with the fan on all day.
But I kept the three things again today. Up at 7, even though I didn't want to. Idli at the mess, a full plate, not just coffee. And the walk: twenty minutes round the lake with Sabina, who doesn't let me skip. She talked about her cat; I mostly listened.
Did any of it fix the project? No. Did it fix home? No. But on days I keep the three things, I can at least open the laptop in the afternoon. On days I don't, I can't.
Sabina said that if it still feels this heavy in a while, or gets worse, she'll come with me to the campus counsellor. I said okay. I think I mean it.
Lights off at 11.
Karthik

qa.q: How long was the walk round the lake?
qa.a: Twenty minutes round the lake with Sabina.

qa.q: Why does Karthik keep the three things even without wanting to?
qa.a: Karthik feels low and heavy, but has noticed that on days with sleep, food and a walk, opening the laptop becomes possible, so the routine feels like the one thing still within reach.

qa.q: What would you advise Karthik to do if the heaviness lasts or gets worse?
qa.a: Take Sabina up on the offer and go to the campus counsellor, while keeping the three things going alongside.

qa.q: What might Sabina be thinking as she walks beside Karthik?
qa.a: Sabina probably sees how low Karthik is and chooses steady company over advice, while keeping watch in case more help is needed.

grounding: A young adult under stress keeps sleep, meals and a walk steady despite low motivation, with a counsellor ready if the distress lasts or worsens.

passage: The final exams at the college in Chikmagalur were two weeks away, and Farida's mind was racing. She couldn't focus and didn't feel like eating. But she remembered what her roommate Lavanya had said last semester: "When your head's a mess, look after your body first." So she kept three things steady. Lights off at eleven, even if she hadn't finished. Breakfast in the mess, even if it was only idli and tea. A walk up the coffee estate road every evening, thirty minutes, even on days she didn't want to. Some days she walked slowly, dragging her feet. But she went. By the second week, her thoughts felt less jumbled. She wasn't cheerful. But she was coping. "And if it gets really bad," Lavanya reminded her, "the college counsellor's right there." Farida nodded. "I know. I'll go if it does."

qa.q: What three things did Farida keep steady?
qa.a: Lights off at eleven, breakfast in the mess, and a walk up the coffee estate road every evening.

qa.q: How did Farida feel during the two weeks, and what changed?
qa.a: She felt stressed and scattered at first, with no appetite, but by the second week her thoughts felt less jumbled and she was coping.

qa.q: Why did keeping body basics steady help Farida?
qa.a: Steady sleep, meals and walks supported her mind even when motivation was low, and she knew the counsellor was there if it got severe.

qa.q: How does Lavanya seem to support Farida?

grounding: It shows a young adult under stress who keeps sleep, meals and walks steady despite low motivation, with a counsellor available if distress gets severe.

passage: Diego had been job hunting in Copenhagen for three months. Every rejection email made his stomach drop. Some mornings he didn't want to get out of bed. His flatmate Lars suggested a simple rule: whatever happens, keep the basics. So Diego set an alarm for eight and got up with it, even when he felt heavy. He ate breakfast at the table, not in bed. At four each afternoon he cycled along the canal for half an hour, rain or not. He didn't feel motivated. He just did it. Some days it barely helped. But the days when he skipped were worse. After a month, Lars noticed Diego humming while cooking. "Better?" "A bit. Still stressed." "If it gets really bad, see a doctor, okay?" Diego nodded. "I've already booked a check-up. Just in case."

qa.q: What time did Diego set his alarm for?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: How did Diego feel during the job hunt, and how did the routine affect it?
qa.a: He felt stressed and heavy, his stomach dropping at rejections; the routine didn't remove it but made days less bad, and after a month he felt a bit better.

qa.q: Why was booking a check-up a wise step alongside the routine?
qa.a: Body basics support coping, but a doctor can help if the stress becomes severe or lasting.

qa.q: How does Lars seem to see Diego's change?
qa.a: Lars notices Diego humming and seems glad, while gently reminding him about a doctor.

grounding: It shows a young adult under stress who keeps sleep, meals and exercise steady even when motivation is low, with a doctor as a step if distress lasts.

passage: Mid-semester in the university hostel in Aligarh, the corridor smelled of instant noodles at two in the morning. Farida's assignments had piled up, and her sleep had gone. So had her appetite. Sonali, her neighbour, noticed her skipping the mess three days in a row. "Farida, come eat. Then we'll walk." Farida came, grumbling. After dinner they walked two rounds of the hostel lawn. Sonali said, "Try this week: sleep by midnight, three meals, one walk. Even if you don't feel like it." Farida did. Some nights she lay awake until one. But she stayed in bed. She went to breakfast, half asleep. She walked every evening with Sonali. By Sunday, she was still behind on assignments, but her head felt clearer. "If it gets worse," Sonali said, "we'll go to the health centre together." Farida nodded.

qa.q: How many days in a row did Farida skip the mess?
qa.a: Three days in a row.

qa.q: How was Farida feeling before Sonali stepped in?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and worn out, with no sleep or appetite as assignments piled up.

qa.q: What routine did Sonali suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Sleep by midnight, three meals and one walk; keeping those steady helped Farida's head feel clearer even though work was still behind.

qa.q: How does Sonali seem to feel about Farida?
qa.a: Sonali seems concerned and caring, noticing the skipped meals and offering company and a plan, including the health centre if needed.

grounding: It shows a young adult under stress who keeps sleep, meals and walks steady with a friend's help, and knows to seek the health centre if distress worsens.

passage:
Dear Binita,

Hostel life in exam month is a strange animal. Half my floor lives on instant noodles and three hours of sleep. I was going that way too. Last week I skipped two dinners, slept at four, and on Thursday I sat in the exam hall and read the same question five times.

So I made myself three rules, even when I don't feel like it. Lights off by midnight. Proper meals in the mess, not noodles. And a twenty-minute walk round the campus lake after lunch, no phone.

Some days I really don't want to walk. I go anyway, slowly. It doesn't make the exams easy. But my head is clearer and I'm not crying in the corridor anymore.

Didi, you're the one who told me about the college counsellor. I haven't needed to go, but I've saved the number, and if this ever feels too heavy for too long, I will.

Your little sister,
Hansa

qa.q: What are Hansa's three rules?
qa.a: Lights off by midnight, proper meals in the mess, and a twenty-minute walk round the campus lake after lunch.

qa.q: How was Hansa feeling before making the three rules?
qa.a: Hansa was exhausted and stressed, skipping dinners, sleeping at four, crying in the corridor and unable to focus in the exam.

qa.q: Why is going on the walk even when unmotivated a wise choice?
qa.a: Keeping sleep, meals and movement steady supports the body, which helps the mind cope even when motivation is low.

qa.q: How might Binita feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Binita would likely feel proud and a little relieved that her sister is looking after herself and has the counsellor's number saved.

grounding: A student under exam stress keeps sleep, meals and a walk steady even without motivation, with a counsellor in mind for heavier times.

passage:
You want to know about that internship summer, Hafsa? Okay, so, it was bad for a bit. I'm Dhruv, and I was twenty-one, in a new city, working for a startup that emailed at midnight.

For three weeks I lived on biscuits, scrolled till two, woke at eight feeling like wet cardboard. My mood was on the floor. I kept waiting for motivation. It never came.

What worked was the boring stuff, done anyway. I set one alarm for bed, eleven thirty, and put my phone in the kitchen. I bought eggs and bread so breakfast was automatic. And I walked to the office instead of taking the metro, thirty minutes each way, even on days I didn't want to.

In ten days I felt like a person again. Not happy all the time. But steady.

And I'll say this straight: if it hadn't lifted, I'd have gone to a doctor. That's not weakness.

qa.q: How long did Dhruv walk to the office each way?
qa.a: Thirty minutes each way.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling during those first three weeks?
qa.a: Dhruv felt low and drained, waking up like wet cardboard, and frustrated that motivation never came.

qa.q: Which of Dhruv's changes might suit another stressed student, and why?
qa.a: A fixed bedtime with the phone out of the room is simple to try; it protects sleep, which helps with everything else.

qa.q: What would change if Dhruv's low mood had not lifted?
qa.a: Dhruv says a doctor would have been the next step, because routines help but lasting distress needs professional help.

grounding: A young adult keeps sleep, meals and walking steady without waiting for motivation, and would see a doctor if distress lasted.

I share a room with Dhruv in the second-year hostel. I'm Pradeep. I can't say what goes on in his head, but I can say what I saw during his final-project month.

The first week he stopped coming to the mess. His light was on at three. He sat on his bed with his laptop and didn't talk much.

Then something changed. He stuck a paper on the wall: "Sleep 12. Breakfast 8. Walk 5." I teased him about it. He just shrugged. At five every evening he went out and walked two rounds of the football ground, even when he looked like he'd rather stay in bed. He came to breakfast with his hair still wet.

He didn't become cheerful. He still sighed at his code. But he spoke more. He laughed at dinner once.

Near the end he told me he'd booked a talk with the campus counsellor, just to check in. I thought that was sensible.

qa.q: What did Dhruv write on the paper stuck to the wall?
qa.a: "Sleep 12. Breakfast 8. Walk 5."

qa.q: What did Pradeep feel when Dhruv started walking every evening?
qa.a: Pradeep was a bit amused at first and teased him, then seemed quietly relieved as Dhruv spoke more and laughed at dinner.

qa.q: What worked about Dhruv's paper on the wall?
qa.a: It made sleep, breakfast and a walk into fixed times he could follow even without motivation, which kept his body steady.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have experienced the month differently from how it looked to Pradeep?
qa.a: Dhruv may have felt heavier inside than he showed, pushing himself to walk, which is why the counsellor check-in made sense.

passage:
"Charu, you've been skipping meals for your exams? Sit, let your Madhav chacha tell you about the worst year of my life.
I was twenty, final year of engineering, and my father was in hospital for months. I was scared all the time. I stopped sleeping properly. I ate biscuits for dinner. I told myself I'd rest after exams.
By December I couldn't think straight. A professor, an old man with kind eyes, said to me, 'Madhav, you can't control the hospital. You can control when you sleep, what you eat and whether you walk.'
So I made rules. Bed by eleven. Dal-rice at the mess, every meal. A walk around the campus lake at six, even when I didn't feel like it.
It didn't fix my father. But I could think again. And when it got too heavy one night, the same professor took me to the college doctor. That helped too."

qa.q: Where did young Madhav walk every evening?
qa.a: He walked around the campus lake at six.

qa.q: How was young Madhav feeling by December?
qa.a: He felt frightened and worn out, unable to think straight after months of poor sleep and meals while his father was in hospital.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Madhav's story, and why did it help?
qa.a: A professor told him to control sleep, food and walking; keeping those basics steady let him think again, and when it got too heavy the professor took him to the college doctor.

qa.q: How might the professor have seen young Madhav?
qa.a: The professor probably saw a frightened student falling apart and felt concern, choosing practical kindness and later a doctor's help.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a young adult under heavy stress keeping sleep, meals and walks steady, and seeing a doctor when it grew too heavy.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded the lanes around Wasim's hostel in Guwahati, and the power kept failing. His internship report was due in ten days, and the stress sat in his chest like a stone. He didn't feel like eating. He didn't feel like moving. He wanted to lie in bed with his phone until it was over.
His senior Jagdish, who had the room across the corridor, pinned a paper on Wasim's door. It said: Sleep 11. Eat 3 meals. Walk 20 min. That's it.
"You don't have to feel like it," Jagdish said. "You just do it."
So on rainy mornings they walked the covered corridor, twenty laps. At dinner, even when the mess food was cold, Wasim ate the full plate.
By the end of the week he was still stressed, but steadier. When he admitted one night that the stone never lifted, Jagdish said, "If it stays like that, we see the college counsellor together."

qa.q: What did Jagdish's paper on the door say?
qa.a: It said: Sleep 11. Eat 3 meals. Walk 20 min. That's it.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel before the routine started?
qa.a: He felt heavily stressed, with a stone in his chest, and didn't feel like eating or moving.

qa.q: Why does the plan work even when Wasim has no motivation?
qa.a: It doesn't rely on feeling like it; steady sleep, meals and walking support his body, and if the heaviness lasts, seeing the counsellor is the next step.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel watching Wasim do the laps?
qa.a: Jagdish probably feels relieved and caring, glad his simple rules are giving Wasim something steady to hold on to.

grounding: It shows a young adult under stress keeping sleep, meals and a walk steady even when motivation is low, with a counsellor as the step if it lasts.

passage:
The flat in Pune smelled of instant coffee and printer ink. Nirmala had an internship report due Friday and two exams the week after, and for three days she hadn't wanted to do anything at all.
Still, at eleven she shut the laptop. Uma, her flatmate, looked up. "You're sleeping? Now?"
"Eleven, every night. It's the one thing I'm not giving up."
In the morning she ate poha standing up, but she ate it. At five, when the report stalled, she walked twice round the colony garden, past the vegetable carts, without her phone.
It didn't make her happy. It kept her upright. On Thursday she told Uma, "If this heaviness doesn't lift after exams, I'm booking the campus counsellor." Uma said she'd go with her if she wanted.

qa.q: What time does Nirmala shut the laptop every night?
qa.a: At eleven she shut the laptop, every night.

qa.q: Why does Nirmala keep her routine even when she doesn't want to do anything?
qa.a: She feels stressed and heavy, and holding on to sleep, meals and a walk gives her something steady when motivation is low.

qa.q: What part of Nirmala's plan shows good judgement beyond routine?
qa.a: She plans to see the campus counsellor if the heaviness doesn't lift, recognising that routine alone might not be enough.
